title: DAVID CAME HOME TO JERUSALEM… BUT TEN WOMEN WERE NEVER ALLOWED TO COME HOME TO THEIR LIVES AGAIN
paragraphs: DAVID CAME HOME TO JERUSALEM… BUT TEN WOMEN WERE NEVER ALLOWED TO COME HOME TO THEIR LIVES AGAIN

The King Reclaimed His Throne. His Son Was Dead. But Behind the Palace Doors, Ten Women Were Left to Carry the Shame of a Sin They Did Not Choose. And What Happened to Them Reveals a Heartbreaking Truth About Human Failure—and Why We Desperately Need Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses that make you shout.
There are Bible verses that make you weep.
And then there are Bible verses that make you close your Bible for a moment because what you just read is so disturbing that you almost wish you hadn't seen it.
This is one of them.
A king returned to his palace.
A rebellion had been crushed.
The throne was restored.
The kingdom could finally breathe again.
But somewhere inside that royal residence, ten women were about to discover that the end of a national tragedy did not mean the end of their personal suffering.
They had already endured something terrible.
Something humiliating.
Something they never should have been forced to experience.
And now, instead of being restored to ordinary life, they would spend the remainder of their days in seclusion.
Not because Scripture tells us they had committed a crime.
Not because God had pronounced them guilty.
But because powerful men had made decisions, and these women were left living with the consequences.
Listen carefully.
Sometimes the person who suffers the longest is not the person who committed the sin.
And if that sentence touches something buried inside you, stay with me.
Because this story is not merely about David, Absalom, or ten forgotten women.
It is about the devastating reach of sin, the limitations of even Israel's greatest kings, and the Savior who came into a broken world to do what no earthly throne could accomplish.
It is about what happens when the battle ends, but the wounded are still bleeding.
And it is about the difference between a king who returns to his palace and the King who comes looking for the brokenhearted.
The Bible says:

"So David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood."
— 2 Samuel 20:3, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
"So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood."
Until the day of their death.
Not for a week.
Not until the political crisis passed.
Not until Jerusalem recovered.
For the rest of their lives.
And the most haunting detail?
Scripture never tells us their names.
Ten women.
Ten human lives.
Ten stories of suffering.
And not one name preserved in this account.
Yet God allowed their suffering to remain recorded in Scripture, where generations of readers would encounter it.
Perhaps the most important question is not simply what happened to them.
Perhaps it is what this passage reveals about the terrible consequences of sin—and whether we have learned to see the people those consequences leave behind.
To understand the tragedy, we must return to the rebellion that nearly destroyed David's kingdom.
Absalom was David's son.
Handsome. Charismatic. Ambitious.
He knew how to win the hearts of people.
He stood near the city gate, listened to grievances, criticized the administration of justice, and presented himself as the leader Israel needed.
Second Samuel 15:6 describes the result:
"So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel."
What a terrifying description.
He did not begin by seizing the throne with a sword.
He began by capturing public affection.
And eventually, he moved against his own father.
David fled Jerusalem.
The king who had defeated Goliath was now running from his own son.
The warrior who had survived Saul's pursuit was escaping a rebellion from inside his family.
The man who once sang of God's deliverance was walking toward the wilderness while his kingdom fractured behind him.
And before leaving, David made a decision that would have devastating consequences for ten women.
Second Samuel 15:16 tells us that David left ten concubines behind to keep the palace.

In the ancient royal household, a concubine was a woman in a recognized but lower-status relationship with the king than a principal wife. Such women often had far less power to determine their own circumstances.
They were left in Jerusalem.
The king departed.
The rebellion advanced.
And Absalom entered the city.
Then came one of the most disturbing scenes in David's family history.
Ahithophel, Absalom's adviser, gave him counsel designed to make reconciliation with David politically impossible.
He urged Absalom to have sexual relations with the concubines his father had left behind.
The purpose was public humiliation.
A declaration of dominance.
A calculated announcement that the son had taken what belonged to his father's royal household.
Second Samuel 16:21 records the counsel.
Then verse 22 tells us:
"So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel."
— 2 Samuel 16:22, KJV
Imagine the horror of that moment.
A rooftop.
A tent.
A rebellious prince.
A nation watching a public assertion of power.
And ten women caught in the middle of a struggle they did not create.

The passage does not describe their individual responses or establish that they consented. Given the circumstances of royal power and political coercion, we must not casually assume that they had meaningful freedom to refuse.
Nor should we turn their suffering into spectacle.
The text emphasizes Absalom's deliberate public act of humiliation against his father. The women were placed at the center of that act.
They were not political advisers plotting a rebellion.
They were not generals commanding an army.
They were not the ones who conceived the plan.
Yet their bodies became instruments in a war between powerful men.
And here is where the story becomes even more painful.
The rooftop was not an accidental location.
Years earlier, David had walked upon the roof of his palace and seen Bathsheba bathing.
That encounter led to David taking Bathsheba, committing adultery, and arranging the death of her husband, Uriah.
The prophet Nathan confronted David and announced that the consequences of his sin would reach into his own household.
In 2 Samuel 12:11, Nathan declared:

"Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun."
The events involving Absalom deliberately echo that warning.
David's secret wrongdoing was followed by public humiliation within his own household.
But we must understand something crucial.
The fulfillment of a prophetic judgment does not mean that God morally approved of Absalom's wicked actions.
Scripture repeatedly distinguishes God's sovereign purposes from the sinful intentions of human beings.
Absalom was responsible for his conduct.
Ahithophel was responsible for his counsel.
And David was responsible for his earlier sins.
The ten women must not be blamed merely because they suffered within the consequences of those sins.
This distinction matters.
Because wounded people have endured enough without being told that someone else's evil somehow proves their own guilt.
A child who grows up in the wreckage of a parent's betrayal is not automatically guilty of the parent's sin.
A spouse devastated by another person's unfaithfulness does not become morally responsible for the betrayal.
A person who has been abused does not become impure or spiritually worthless because someone violated their dignity.
And someone living with consequences they never chose should never be told that their suffering makes them less worthy of compassion.
There is a Hebrew word worth examining here.

In 2 Samuel 20:3, the Hebrew text describes David placing the women in a guarded or restricted setting using the expression בֵּית־מִשְׁמֶר (bêt-mišmer), meaning a place of custody, confinement, or guarded keeping.
The verse also says:
וַיְכַלְכְּלֵם (vaykhalkelēm)
Meaning, "and he provided for them" or "and he sustained them."
And then comes the devastating conclusion:
צְרֻרוֹת עַד־יוֹם מֻתָן (tserurot ʿad-yom mutan)
A phrase describing their being shut away or confined until the day of their death.
The passage ends by describing them as living in widowhood.
The Hebrew word אַלְמְנוּת (ʾalmenût) refers to widowhood.
They were not literally widows in the ordinary sense, because David was still alive.
Rather, they lived in a widow-like condition, deprived of an ongoing marital relationship with the king.
David continued to provide for them materially.
But he did not resume sexual relations with them.
The text does not explicitly explain every motive behind his decision.

Some interpreters understand his action in relation to the royal household's sexual boundaries and the political disgrace surrounding Absalom's actions. Others emphasize the severe social restrictions imposed on the women.
We should not pretend to know more than Scripture reveals.
What we do know is heartbreaking enough.
They were provided for.
But they remained secluded.
They survived.
But their former lives were not restored.
And the Bible records no later reversal of their circumstances.
Think about that.
It is possible to have food and still be lonely.
It is possible to have shelter and still feel imprisoned.
It is possible to be physically protected and still carry wounds that nobody has addressed.
It is possible for the people around you to say, "At least you're alive," while you are silently grieving the life you once knew.
Somebody reading this understands.
You have survived something that changed you.
People see you working.
Smiling.
Cooking.
Going to church.
Taking care of your family.
Posting photographs.
Answering messages.
And they assume you have recovered.
But they do not see what happens when the house becomes quiet.
They do not know which memories return.
They do not know how often you have wondered whether you will ever feel like yourself again.
And perhaps the hardest part is that the people responsible for the damage seem to have moved forward while you are still carrying the aftermath.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
What happened to you is not the whole truth about who you are.
The cruelty of another person does not have the authority to define your worth before God.
And the silence surrounding your pain does not mean your suffering is invisible to Him.
But there is another difficult truth in this story.
David was not an unbelieving pagan king.
He was the Lord's anointed.
A man who wrote psalms.
A man who knew repentance.
A man who experienced mercy.
A man whose life contained extraordinary faith and terrible moral failure.
And that should sober every Christian.
Spiritual history does not make someone incapable of causing harm.
Public ministry does not guarantee private righteousness.
Knowing the language of worship does not excuse injustice.
Being used by God does not place a person beyond accountability.
David's life teaches us that genuine faith and serious failure can exist in the same human story.
That is not an excuse for sin.
It is a warning against spiritual pride.
And when we examine David's household, the warning becomes almost unbearable.
Amnon sexually violated his half-sister Tamar.
David became angry, but the biblical narrative does not describe him securing justice for her.
Absalom eventually murdered Amnon.
Then Absalom rebelled against David.
And during that rebellion, the ten concubines were subjected to another act of sexual humiliation within the royal household.
Different events.
Different individuals.
Different responsibilities.
But an unmistakable pattern of family devastation.
Sin does not remain neatly confined to the moment in which it is committed.
It can fracture trust.
Distort relationships.
Corrupt authority.
And leave generations struggling with consequences they never anticipated.
This is why repentance cannot be reduced to feeling bad after being exposed.
The Hebrew word commonly associated with turning or returning is שׁוּב (shuv).
It carries the basic sense of turning back or returning, and in prophetic calls to repentance it describes turning toward the Lord.
True repentance is not merely saying, "I'm sorry."
It means turning away from sin and toward God.
Where possible, it also produces the fruit of responsibility, truthfulness, and making wrongs right.
David himself understood the seriousness of confession.
In Psalm 51:4, he cried:
"Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight."
That statement emphasizes the ultimate offense of sin against God; it does not erase the real human victims of David's actions.
Psalm 51 also says:
"A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."
— Psalm 51:17, KJV
And yet the story of the ten women reminds us that even when a sinner receives forgiveness, the earthly consequences of sin may remain painfully real.
Forgiveness does not mean that the damage never happened.
Grace does not make accountability unnecessary.
And reconciliation should never be demanded from someone whose safety is still at risk.
There is a difference between extending forgiveness and returning to an unsafe situation.
There is a difference between trusting God and pretending that abuse did not occur.
There is a difference between Christian compassion and protecting an offender from the consequences of wrongdoing.
The church must never confuse those things.
Because the God of Scripture is not indifferent to the vulnerable.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
And Psalm 147:3 says:
"He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds."
Notice the language.
He binds up wounds.
That is not the language of a God who mocks suffering.
It is the language of compassionate care.
But the story does not end with the brokenness of David's household.
Because centuries later, another Son of David would come.
Not a son who seized the throne through rebellion.
Not a king who used vulnerable people to demonstrate political power.
Not a ruler who sought to protect his glory at the expense of the wounded.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Messiah.
The true and greater Son of David.
The One whose kingdom would not be established through exploitation, but through righteousness, sacrificial love, and the triumph of His resurrection.
When Jesus began His public ministry, He read from the prophet Isaiah.
Luke 4:18 records His words:

"The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised."

This wording follows the KJV. The phrase "to heal the brokenhearted" reflects the traditional textual form behind that translation, while many modern critical Greek editions of Luke omit that particular clause. The theme of God's care for the brokenhearted is nevertheless explicit in Isaiah 61 and elsewhere in Scripture.
The Greek word ἄφεσις (aphesis), used in Luke 4:18, carries the meaning of release, liberation, or forgiveness, depending on context.
And the word τεθραυσμένους (tethrausmenous) describes those who have been crushed or broken.
Jesus announced good news to people who desperately needed it.
He came to bring the saving reign of God into a world filled with sin, oppression, guilt, grief, and death.
His mission was not merely to improve human circumstances.
He came to save sinners and ultimately make all things new.
And this is where the contrast becomes breathtaking.
David returned to Jerusalem after fleeing a rebellion.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing He would be rejected.
David reclaimed his royal residence.
Jesus was led outside the city to be crucified.
David's household bore the consequences of sin.
Jesus, though sinless, bore the sins of His people.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."
The cross was not another example of an innocent person being forgotten by God.
It was the place where the sinless Son willingly gave Himself to accomplish redemption.
Jesus was not overcome by evil as a helpless victim of circumstances.
He laid down His life.
John 10:18 records His declaration:
"No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself."
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final word.
This is the Gospel.
Not that suffering is imaginary.
Not that consequences disappear.
Not that every earthly injustice is corrected before we die.
But that Jesus Christ has entered our broken world, conquered death, and secured forgiveness and eternal life for those who belong to Him.
The King who died for sinners is alive.
And His resurrection guarantees that God's final restoration will be greater than anything this fallen world can accomplish.
Revelation 21:4 gives this promise:
"And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."
Can you imagine that?
No more tears.
No more death.
No more sorrow.
No more pain.
No more victims abandoned to the cruelty of a fallen world.
No more graves.
No more nights spent wondering whether God has forgotten.
The Bible does not tell us the eternal destiny of David's ten concubines.
It does not tell us whether they personally experienced healing, freedom, or restored relationships during their remaining earthly years.
We must not invent a happy ending that Scripture does not provide.
But their unfinished story can awaken our longing for the perfect justice and restoration that only God can bring.
And perhaps that is one of the reasons this verse feels so unbearable.
We want someone to open the doors.
We want someone to say, "You have suffered enough."
We want their names to be remembered.
We want the wrongs to be acknowledged.
We want the women to have the final word instead of the men who controlled their circumstances.
But the narrative moves forward.
And their story disappears from view.
That silence should not make us indifferent.
It should make us more attentive to people who are suffering quietly around us.
Because there may be someone sitting beside you in church who has survived a violation they have never spoken about.
Someone whose marriage collapsed because of another person's choices.
Someone carrying childhood wounds into adulthood.
Someone who smiles while silently grieving.
Someone who has been told to forgive but has never been given the space to speak honestly about what happened.
Someone who believes Jesus can forgive the person who hurt them but wonders whether Jesus has any compassion left for them.
If that is you, please hear this.
Jesus does not require you to deny your pain before you come to Him.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony of complete healing when you are still struggling.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to pretend that everything is fine.
And you do not have to earn the compassion of Christ by becoming emotionally strong enough to impress Him.
Come to Him truthfully.
Come with the tears.
Come with the questions.
Come with the confusion.
Come with the anger that needs His wisdom.
Come with the guilt that needs His forgiveness.
Come with the wounds that need His care.
He is not frightened by the truth about your life.
Matthew 11:28 records His invitation:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
But we must also be careful not to turn this story into a message only for those who have been wounded.
There is a warning here for those who have wounded others.
Perhaps you have used your authority selfishly.
Perhaps you have betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you have minimized another person's pain because acknowledging it would require you to confront your own sin.
Perhaps you have hidden behind religious language while refusing accountability.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that because God forgives, the people you hurt should simply move on.
Do not confuse God's mercy with permission to remain unchanged.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness leads us toward repentance.
And 1 John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Confession means bringing sin into the light.
Repentance means turning away from it.
And genuine faith produces a changed direction of life.
If you have harmed someone, do not use the language of grace to demand their silence.
Do not use Scripture to pressure them into restoring access to their life.
Seek forgiveness from God.
Accept appropriate accountability.
Make restitution where possible.
Respect boundaries.
And let the fruit of repentance speak more loudly than religious promises.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could become comfortable with the sins that nailed Him to the cross.
He came to save us from sin, not to teach us how to disguise it.
And if you are the person who has been hurt, understand this distinction.
The call for sinners to repent does not place the responsibility for their repentance upon you.
You cannot repent for another person.
You cannot force someone to become honest.
You cannot heal a heart that refuses correction.
But you can bring your own heart before the Lord.
You can seek wise and trustworthy support.
You can pursue safety.
You can receive help without shame.
And you can begin to discover that the worst thing someone did to you does not have to become the final chapter of your identity.
There is something else I cannot ignore.
David's ten concubines were remembered in the biblical account primarily through what happened to them.
We know their number.
We know their status.
We know their seclusion.
But we do not know their names.
And perhaps some of you know exactly what it feels like to have your entire life reduced to one painful event.
The divorced woman.
The abused child.
The betrayed husband.
The abandoned mother.
The recovering addict.
The person who failed publicly.
The one who went through depression.
The one whose family fell apart.
The one everybody whispers about.
But you are more than the worst chapter of your story.
You are not merely the scandal.
You are not merely the wound.
You are not merely the failure.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
This does not promise instant freedom from every traumatic memory or earthly consequence.
It proclaims the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
His grace gives sinners a new standing before God and begins a life of renewal that will ultimately be completed in glory.
That is why we keep returning to this message.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because grace erases history.
Not because every story receives a beautiful earthly resolution.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, sustain the brokenhearted, and bring His people into a future that sin cannot destroy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the terrible chapters were never written.
But by refusing to let sin and death write the final sentence for those He redeems.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Who came to mind while you were reading this?
Was it your mother?
Your daughter?
Your sister?
Your husband?
A friend who has stopped attending church?
Someone whose faith has been shaken by betrayal?
Or was it you?
Maybe you have spent years keeping your pain behind a closed door.
Maybe people have called you strong because they never knew how close you were to collapsing.
Maybe you have been serving everyone else while quietly wondering when someone will notice that you are hurting too.
Maybe you have been asking God why the people who caused the damage seem to have escaped while you are still living with the consequences.
I cannot answer every question about why God permits particular suffering.
And I will not insult your pain by pretending that a few comforting sentences can explain everything.
But I can tell you what the Gospel reveals.
God did not remain distant from a suffering world.
In Jesus Christ, the eternal Son entered human history.
He knew rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew injustice.
He knew suffering.
He died for sinners.
He rose in victory.
And He will return to judge the world in righteousness.
That means evil does not have ultimate authority.
Human power does not have ultimate authority.
The grave does not have ultimate authority.
Jesus Christ does.
And the hands that were pierced for our redemption belong to the risen King.
So if you are exhausted, do not mistake exhaustion for abandonment.
If you are grieving, do not mistake tears for unbelief.
If you are struggling to trust again, do not confuse your need for wisdom and safety with a lack of faith.
And if you have wandered from Christ because of your own sin, do not imagine that repentance is beneath you or that grace is beyond His power.
Turn to Him.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you have repaired yourself.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Today.
The Gospel does not say, "Become perfect and then come."
It calls sinners to repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
And it assures those who come to Him that His saving grace is sufficient.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the ashamed sinner who needs forgiveness.
There is compassion in the heart of Jesus for the wounded person who needs comfort.
And there is hope in the resurrection of Jesus for everyone who wonders whether darkness will last forever.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish religious words.
Not merely to collect reactions.
Not merely to build a page.
But to keep pointing people toward the Scriptures, toward repentance, toward the cross, toward the empty tomb, and toward a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
Because someone scrolling through Facebook tonight may be one message away from opening a Bible again.
Someone who has stopped praying may be reminded that God hears the brokenhearted.
Someone carrying secret guilt may finally understand the need to repent.
Someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy may begin to distinguish the failures of people from the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
And someone who has never understood the Gospel may hear the good news of salvation for the first time.
If this article has touched something deep within you, please do not feel pressured to reveal details you are not ready to share.
You can simply write "Christ is still healing me."
If you are convicted about sin you have been hiding, you can write "Jesus, have mercy on me."
And if you have a testimony of how the Lord carried you through suffering, consider sharing it. Your words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
You do not have to tell your entire story publicly for your faith to be real.
Sometimes a simple, sincere prayer is enough to begin an honest conversation.
And please think about someone who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to confront publicly.
But someone who needs to know that the compassion of Christ has not run out.
Send this article privately if that would be more appropriate.
One thoughtful share may bring Scripture into the life of someone who would never intentionally search for a Christian article.
We want this to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, not empty religious performance.
A place where repentance is preached without forgetting mercy.
Where grace is celebrated without excusing sin.
Where the wounded are treated with compassion.
And where Jesus Christ—not personalities, popularity, or financial success—remains at the center.
Not because every wound will disappear after reading it.
But because there may come another difficult night when you need to remember that the Lord sees what others overlook.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Word of God, grow in prayer, understand the Gospel, strengthen their faith, and continue following Jesus beyond a single emotional moment.
They are free because biblical encouragement and discipleship resources should remain accessible to people who may not have the means to purchase them.
But keeping resources available and expanding this work also requires practical support.
And that is where I want to speak to you sincerely.
Not because you owe us anything.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price for our redemption. No monthly payment can add anything to His finished work.
But believers can glorify God through voluntary generosity when their giving is motivated by love, truth, and a sincere desire to serve others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
It can help sustain the work and support its expansion.
It is an additional opportunity to give freely toward a ministry whose work you believe is worthwhile.
You are not less faithful.
You are not less valuable.
You are not less welcome.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, encouragement, and willingness to share biblical truth also matter.
These items can serve as personal reminders of faith, meaningful gifts, and tools for encouraging others.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered teaching and free discipleship resources reaching people who need them.
Because this mission is bigger than a page.
It is about the Gospel being heard.
The truth being understood.
Sinners being called to repentance.
Believers being strengthened.
The brokenhearted being reminded of God's compassion.
And Jesus Christ being glorified.
Before you leave, return with me one last time to that palace in Jerusalem.
The rebellion was over.
David was home.
The throne had been restored.
The king had returned.
But ten women remained behind closed doors.
The Bible gives us no scene in which those doors are opened again for them.
No record of a celebration.
No account of restored freedom.
No final testimony in their own voices.
Just the haunting words:
"Shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood."
And perhaps this is where the story should change the way we look at people.
Because somewhere around us, there are still people living behind invisible doors.
Doors of grief.
Doors of shame.
Doors of betrayal.
Doors of fear.
Doors of consequences they did not choose.
Some of them are sitting in our churches.
Some are living inside our homes.
Some are among our closest friends.
And some are reading these very words.
May we never become so fascinated by the victories of powerful people that we forget the suffering of those left behind.
May we never preach forgiveness in a way that silences victims.
May we never celebrate grace while refusing to confront evil.
May we never confuse outward survival with inward restoration.
And may we never forget that the greatest hope of the wounded is not found in the perfection of earthly kings, religious leaders, or human institutions.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
The righteous King.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The One who forgives repentant sinners.
The One who cares for the brokenhearted.
The One who will judge with perfect righteousness.
The One who will make all things new.
So bring Him your guilt.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your unfinished story.
Above all, do not leave this story merely thinking about ten women who suffered in ancient Jerusalem.
Leave thinking about the Savior who entered human history to redeem a people for Himself.
Because the final hope of the Christian faith is not that every earthly palace will eventually become safe.
It is that Jesus Christ will return, evil will be judged, death will be defeated forever, and those who belong to Him will dwell in His presence.

And until that day, may we proclaim His truth, practice His compassion, protect the vulnerable, pursue holiness, and carry the hope of His Gospel into places where people have nearly forgotten what hope feels like.
The world may remember the throne that was restored, but heaven's King teaches us to care about the wounded people the victory left behind.
